theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Deriving and Applying the BJT Models

The transconductance comes straight from the exponential law. Differentiating I_C = I_S e^(V_BE/V_T) with respect to V_BE gives I_S e^(V_BE/V_T) / V_T, which is simply I_C / V_T. The same law shows that V_BE rises by V_T ln 10, about 60 mV, for every tenfold increase in collector current, and by V_T ln 2, about 18 mV, when the current doubles. Expanding e^(v_be/V_T) as 1 + v_be/V_T + ... shows why the linear model needs v_be much smaller than V_T: at 5 mV the neglected square term is already about 10 % of the linear term.

theoryAdd.plainText: g_m = di_C/dv_BE = I_C / V_T;  ΔV_BE = V_T·ln(I_C2 / I_C1)

theoryAdd.text: In the Ebers-Moll equations each junction current follows the diode law, I_F = I_ES (e^(V_BE/V_T) − 1) for the emitter diode and I_R = I_CS (e^(V_BC/V_T) − 1) for the collector diode. The terminal currents are I_C = α_F I_F − I_R and I_E = I_F − α_R I_R. Reciprocity requires α_F I_ES = α_R I_CS = I_S. Because the collector is large and lightly doped, α_R is small (roughly 0.1 to 0.5), so the reverse-active current gain β_R = α_R / (1 − α_R) is usually below 1; this is why a transistor with collector and emitter swapped is a poor amplifier.

rows: V_BE ≈ 0.8 V, V_CE(sat) ≈ 0.2 V, I_C < β I_B
Roles swapped; β_R well below β_F

theoryAdd.text:
Worked example 1 - is the transistor saturated?
Given: V_BB = 3.3 V, R_B = 10 kΩ, V_CC = 5 V, R_C = 1 kΩ, β = 80
Assume active: I_B = (3.3 − 0.7) / 10 kΩ = 0.26 mA
  I_C = β I_B = 80 × 0.26 mA = 20.8 mA
  V_CE = 5 − 20.8 mA × 1 kΩ = −15.8 V  -> impossible
So the BJT is saturated: V_CE = 0.2 V
  I_C(sat) = (5 − 0.2) / 1 kΩ = 4.8 mA
  Forced beta = I_C / I_B = 4.8 / 0.26 = 18.5 (less than 80)
  Minimum base current for saturation = 4.8 mA / 80 = 60 µA
Converting between the model families (common-emitter h-parameters on the left):
items: h_fe = β and h_ie = r_π, so g_m = h_fe / h_ie; for example h_fe = 100 and h_ie = 2.5 kΩ give g_m = 40 mA/V, which at V_T = 25 mV means I_C = 1 mA.
h_oe = 1 / r_o, so a data-sheet h_oe of 20 µS corresponds to r_o = 50 kΩ in the hybrid-π model.
Common-base values follow from the CE ones: h_ib = h_ie / (1 + h_fe), which is r_e, and h_fb = −h_fe / (1 + h_fe), which is −α.
h_re and h_fe are dimensionless, h_ie is in ohms and h_oe is in siemens; that mix of units is why they are called hybrid parameters.

theoryAdd.latex: A_i = \frac{h_{fe}}{1 + h_{oe} R_L}, \quad Z_i = h_{ie} - h_{re} A_i R_L
theoryAdd.plainText: A_i = h_fe / (1 + h_oe·R_L);  Z_i = h_ie − h_re·A_i·R_L = h_ie − h_re·h_fe·R_L / (1 + h_oe·R_L)

theoryAdd.text: Writing the CE gain as A_v = −g_m R_C = −I_C R_C / V_T shows that the gain equals the DC voltage dropped across R_C divided by V_T: a 5 V drop gives about −200 at V_T = 25 mV, whatever the individual values of I_C and R_C. The largest gain a single transistor can give, with only its own r_o as load, is the intrinsic gain g_m r_o = V_A / V_T, a few thousand. At high frequencies the hybrid-π model adds C_π between base and emitter and C_µ between base and collector, and the transition frequency where the short-circuit current gain falls to 1 is f_T = g_m / (2π (C_π + C_µ)).

Frequent slips in model questions: using r_e = 26 mV / I_E with I_E in amperes and quoting the answer in ohms without the factor 1000; taking g_m = I_B / V_T instead of I_C / V_T; forgetting R_L in parallel with R_C in the AC load; using −R_C / r_e when R_E is not bypassed; and trusting I_C = β I_B without first checking that V_CE is above V_CE(sat).

questions.questionText: The Ebers-Moll model of a BJT is valid in which operating regions?
options: All four: forward-active, saturation, cut-off and reverse-active
questions.explanation: The Ebers-Moll model uses the full diode law for both junctions with two dependent sources, so it describes all four regions; piecewise models are region-specific.

questions.questionText: The Ebers-Moll large-signal model of a BJT consists of:
options: A single diode in series with a resistor
Two back-to-back diodes, each paralleled by a current-controlled current source
A voltage-controlled voltage source and an output resistance
A 0.7 V battery and a resistor r_e only
questions.explanation: Ebers-Moll represents the base-emitter and base-collector junctions as diodes, each shunted by a dependent source carrying α times the other junction's diode current.

questions.questionText: A silicon BJT in the active region has I_S = 10^-14 A. Using I_C = I_S e^(V_BE/V_T) with V_T = 26 mV, the collector current at V_BE = 0.65 V is about:
For a BJT obeying I_C = I_S e^(V_BE/V_T) with V_T = 26 mV, by how much must V_BE increase to raise I_C tenfold?
questions.explanation: ΔV_BE = V_T ln(10) = 26 mV × 2.303 = 59.9 mV, about 60 mV per decade of current.

questions.questionText: A BJT is operating at I_C = 1 mA. With V_T = 26 mV, the increase in V_BE required to double the collector current to 2 mA is about:
In a base-driven switch, V_BB = 5 V is applied through R_B = 20 kΩ; the collector is fed from V_CC = 10 V through R_C = 2 kΩ, and β = 100 (V_BE = 0.7 V, V_CE(sat) = 0.2 V). The transistor is:
options: Active, with I_C ≈ 21.5 mA and V_CE ≈ −33 V
Active, with I_C ≈ 2.15 mA and V_CE ≈ 5.7 V
Saturated, with I_C ≈ 4.9 mA and V_CE ≈ 0.2 V
Cut off, with I_C ≈ 0 and V_CE = 10 V
questions.explanation: I_B = (5 − 0.7)/20 kΩ = 215 µA, so β I_B = 21.5 mA would need V_CE = 10 − 43 = −33 V, which is impossible. The BJT saturates: I_C = (10 − 0.2)/2 kΩ = 4.9 mA.

questions.questionText: A fixed-bias silicon BJT has V_CC = 12 V, R_B = 565 kΩ, R_C = 3 kΩ and β = 100 (V_BE = 0.7 V). The Q-point (I_CQ, V_CEQ) is:
A saturated BJT switch carries I_C = 5 mA with a base current of 0.5 mA. Its forced beta is:
questions.explanation: Forced beta = I_C/I_B = 5 mA / 0.5 mA = 10; in saturation this is always below the active-region β.

questions.questionText: In the large-signal piecewise model, a BJT in cut-off is represented between collector and emitter by:
questions.explanation: In cut-off both junctions are reverse biased and all currents are practically zero, so the collector-emitter path is an open switch.

questions.questionText: When a BJT is operated in the reverse-active mode (collector and emitter roles interchanged), its current gain is:
options: Much smaller than the forward β, usually below 1
Infinite, because the base current becomes zero
questions.explanation: The lightly doped, large collector is a poor emitter, so α_R is small (about 0.1 to 0.5) and β_R = α_R/(1 − α_R) is usually less than 1.

questions.questionText: In the Ebers-Moll model, reciprocity requires α_F I_ES = α_R I_CS = I_S. A transistor has I_S = 2 × 10^-15 A and reverse alpha α_R = 0.4. Its collector-diode saturation current I_CS is:
questions.explanation: I_CS = I_S/α_R = 2 × 10^-15 / 0.4 = 5 × 10^-15 A; the collector diode has the larger saturation current because α_R is small.

questions.questionText: A CE stage (emitter bypassed) runs at I_C = 2 mA with V_T = 25 mV and Early voltage V_A = 100 V. R_C = 5 kΩ and the load R_L = 5 kΩ. Including r_o, the voltage gain is about:
At room temperature (V_T = 25 mV), a BJT biased at I_C = 0.5 mA has a transconductance of:
questions.explanation: g_m = I_C/V_T = 0.5 mA / 25 mV = 20 mA/V.

questions.questionText: A BJT with β = 150 is biased at I_C = 1.5 mA (V_T = 25 mV). Its hybrid-π input resistance r_π is:
The quiescent base current of a BJT is 10 µA. With V_T = 26 mV, the small-signal resistance r_π is:
questions.explanation: r_π = V_T/I_B = 26 mV / 10 µA = 2.6 kΩ.

questions.questionText: A BJT has an Early voltage V_A = 100 V and is biased at I_C = 2 mA. Its small-signal output resistance r_o is:
questions.explanation: r_o = V_A/I_C = 100 V / 2 mA = 50 kΩ.

questions.questionText: For a BJT with V_A = 50 V at room temperature (V_T = 25 mV), the intrinsic voltage gain g_m r_o is:
questions.explanation: g_m r_o = (I_C/V_T)(V_A/I_C) = V_A/V_T = 50/0.025 = 2000, independent of the bias current.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the hybrid-π parameters of a BJT is correct?
options: g_m depends only on I_C and temperature, not on β
r_π is independent of the bias current
r_o decreases when the Early voltage increases
questions.explanation: g_m = I_C/V_T contains no β; r_π = β/g_m falls as I_C rises, and r_o = V_A/I_C grows with V_A.

questions.questionText: A BJT with β = 99 is biased at I_E = 2.5 mA (V_T = 25 mV). Its r_e and r_π are respectively:
The small-signal (linear) models of a BJT are valid only when:
options: The AC base-emitter voltage is larger than 0.7 V
The AC base-emitter voltage is much smaller than V_T (a few millivolts)
questions.explanation: The exponential i_C-v_BE law is well approximated by its tangent only if v_be ≪ V_T ≈ 25 mV.

questions.questionText: The thermal voltage V_T = kT/q at T = 300 K (k = 1.38 × 10^-23 J/K, q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C) is about:
In the high-frequency hybrid-π model of a BJT, the capacitances C_π and C_µ represent:
options: The base-emitter and base-collector junction capacitances
The coupling and bypass capacitors of the amplifier
The collector-emitter and collector-substrate capacitances only
The capacitances of the DC power supply
questions.explanation: C_π (diffusion plus depletion) sits between base and emitter, C_µ (depletion) between base and collector; external coupling and bypass capacitors are separate.

questions.questionText: A BJT biased at I_C = 1 mA (V_T = 25 mV) has C_π = 11 pF and C_µ = 1 pF. Its transition frequency f_T = g_m / (2π(C_π + C_µ)) is about:
questions.explanation: g_m = 1 mA/25 mV = 40 mA/V; f_T = 0.04 / (2π × 12 pF) = 531 MHz (using C_π alone would give 579 MHz).

questions.questionText: When drawing the small-signal AC equivalent circuit of a BJT amplifier, the DC supply V_CC and the large coupling/bypass capacitors are replaced by:
questions.explanation: An ideal DC source has zero AC voltage and a large capacitor has negligible reactance at signal frequency, so both become shorts in the AC model.

questions.questionText: A BJT is biased at I_C = 2 mA (V_T = 25 mV) and a 5 mV peak signal is applied between base and emitter. The resulting peak AC collector current is about:
questions.explanation: i_c = g_m v_be = (2 mA/25 mV) × 5 mV = 80 mA/V × 5 mV = 0.4 mA.

questions.questionText: The CE h-parameter h_oe is measured in:
questions.explanation: h_oe = i_c/v_ce with the input open; a current divided by a voltage is an admittance, in siemens.

questions.questionText: Which pair of CE h-parameters is dimensionless?
questions.explanation: h_re is a voltage ratio and h_fe a current ratio, so both are pure numbers; h_ie is in ohms and h_oe in siemens.

questions.questionText: A CE amplifier uses a transistor with h_fe = 120 and h_ie = 2 kΩ. R_C = 4 kΩ and R_L = 4 kΩ (h_re and h_oe neglected). The voltage gain is:
questions.explanation: AC load = R_C ∥ R_L = 2 kΩ; A_v = −h_fe R_ac/h_ie = −120 × 2 kΩ/2 kΩ = −120.

questions.questionText: A CE transistor has h_fe = 100 and h_oe = 25 µS and drives a load R_L = 4 kΩ. Its current gain A_i = h_fe/(1 + h_oe R_L) is about:
A CE transistor has h_ie = 1.1 kΩ, h_re = 2.5 × 10^-4, h_fe = 50 and h_oe = 25 µS, with R_L = 1 kΩ. Its exact input impedance Z_i = h_ie − h_re h_fe R_L/(1 + h_oe R_L) is about:
questions.explanation: h_oe R_L = 0.025; h_re h_fe R_L/(1.025) = 2.5 × 10^-4 × 50 × 1000/1.025 = 12.2 Ω; Z_i = 1100 − 12.2 = 1088 Ω ≈ 1.09 kΩ. Adding the term instead of subtracting it gives 1.11 kΩ, which is wrong.

questions.questionText: A transistor data sheet gives h_fe = 100 and h_ie = 2.5 kΩ at the operating point. Taking V_T = 25 mV, the collector bias current is about:
questions.explanation: g_m = h_fe/h_ie = 100/2.5 kΩ = 40 mA/V; I_C = g_m V_T = 40 mA/V × 25 mV = 1 mA.

questions.questionText: A transistor has CE current gain h_fe = 99. Its common-base short-circuit current gain h_fb is:
A transistor has h_ie = 2 kΩ and h_fe = 99 in the CE configuration. Its common-base input resistance h_ib is about:
questions.explanation: h_ib = h_ie/(1 + h_fe) = 2000/100 = 20 Ω; this is the emitter resistance r_e.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the h-parameter model of a BJT is NOT correct?
options: Its values depend on the Q-point
It remains accurate at high frequencies without any added capacitances
h_ie and h_fe correspond to r_π and β of the hybrid-π model
h_re and h_oe are often neglected in approximate analysis
questions.explanation: Data-sheet h-parameters are low-frequency, real-valued quantities; they ignore junction capacitances, so they are not valid at high frequencies. The other statements are true.

questions.questionText: A CE stage runs at I_C = 1 mA (V_T = 25 mV) with R_C = 5 kΩ and no external load. The transistor's h_oe is 20 µS. Including h_oe, the voltage gain is about:

A voltage-divider CE amplifier has V_CC = 12 V, R1 = 40 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, R_E = 1 kΩ (fully bypassed), R_C = 4 kΩ and R_L = 4 kΩ. Using the approximate analysis (base current neglected, V_BE = 0.7 V, V_T = 25 mV), the voltage gain is about:
A CE amplifier has R_C = 4.7 kΩ and an unbypassed emitter resistor R_E = 470 Ω. At the Q-point r_e = 13 Ω. The voltage gain is about:
A CE stage with R_C = 10 kΩ has an unbypassed emitter resistance R_E = 1 kΩ, which is much larger than r_e. Its voltage gain is approximately:
questions.explanation: When R_E ≫ r_e, A_v ≈ −R_C/R_E = −10 kΩ/1 kΩ = −10, nearly independent of the transistor.

questions.questionText: A BJT with β = 99 has r_e = 25 Ω and an unbypassed emitter resistor R_E = 500 Ω. The resistance looking into its base is about:

A CE amplifier has an unloaded-source voltage gain A_v = −150, bias resistance R_B = 10 kΩ and r_π = 2.5 kΩ. It is driven by a source with internal resistance R_s = 1 kΩ. The overall gain v_o/v_s is about:
questions.explanation: R_in = R_B ∥ r_π = 10k ∥ 2.5k = 2 kΩ; A_vs = A_v × R_in/(R_in + R_s) = −150 × 2/3 = −100 (using r_π alone gives −107).

questions.questionText: A CE amplifier has R_C = 10 kΩ and the transistor's r_o = 40 kΩ. Its output resistance (looking back into the collector node) is:
The phase difference between the input and output voltages of a common-emitter amplifier at mid-band frequencies is:
questions.explanation: A rise in base voltage raises i_c, increasing the drop across R_C, so the collector voltage falls: the CE stage inverts (negative gain, 180°).

questions.questionText: If the emitter bypass capacitor of a CE amplifier opens (becomes disconnected), then:
options: The voltage gain rises and the input resistance falls
The voltage gain falls and the input resistance rises
Both the voltage gain and input resistance rise
The DC Q-point shifts into saturation
questions.explanation: Without the bypass, R_E appears in the AC emitter circuit: gain drops to about −R_C/(r_e + R_E) and base input resistance rises to (β + 1)(r_e + R_E). The DC bias is unchanged because the capacitor is open for DC anyway.

questions.questionText: In a bypassed CE stage the quiescent voltage drop across R_C is 5 V. With V_T = 25 mV, the voltage gain magnitude (no load) is:
questions.explanation: |A_v| = g_m R_C = I_C R_C/V_T = 5 V/25 mV = 200, whatever the separate values of I_C and R_C.

questions.questionText: An emitter follower has R_E = 1 kΩ (no external load) and r_e = 25 Ω. Its voltage gain is about:
questions.explanation: A_v = R_E/(R_E + r_e) = 1000/1025 = 0.976: slightly less than one with no phase inversion.

questions.questionText: A common-base amplifier runs at I_E = 0.5 mA (V_T = 25 mV). Its input resistance looking into the emitter is about:
questions.explanation: R_in(CB) ≈ r_e = V_T/I_E = 25 mV/0.5 mA = 50 Ω, which is why the CB stage has a very low input resistance.
